title: Inverted Index
summary: The term → document data structure at the core of every search engine, and how raw text becomes something it can query in microseconds.

slides.markdown:
An **inverted index** flips the natural direction of a document collection: instead of "document → the words it contains," it stores "word → the documents that contain it." That flip is what makes "find every document containing 'database'" a direct lookup instead of a scan through every document.

It's the same idea as the index at the back of a textbook — you don't read the whole book to find every mention of a topic, you look the topic up and jump straight to the pages. Every major search engine (Elasticsearch, Lucene, Google's own) is built on this one structure.

slides.sectionTitle: The inverted index: from documents to a term → document map
slides.markdown:
A **forward index** stores documents as-is: `doc1 → "the cat sat on the mat"`. To find every document containing "cat," you'd have to read every document's full text.

An **inverted index** stores the reverse mapping: for each distinct term, the list of documents it appears in — `"cat" → [doc1, doc7, doc23]`. Now finding matches for "cat" is a single lookup by key, no scanning required, the same way looking up a word in a dictionary doesn't require reading every page before it.

This is the foundational trade: it costs more storage and upfront work to build the index, in exchange for near-instant lookups at query time — exactly the trade you want when you index once and query millions of times.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: building an inverted index from a handful of documents
slides.markdown:
![Three documents inverted into a term-to-postings table](assets/inverted-index-build.svg)

Building the index means walking every document once, splitting it into terms, and appending the document's ID to that term's list. "cat" ends up pointing at doc1 and doc3; "ran" points at doc2 and doc3; common words like "the" would point at all three (which is exactly why stop words get filtered — more on that next).

Notice this is a one-time cost per document: once built, answering "which documents mention cat?" no longer touches the document text at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Tokenization, stemming, stop words: preparing text for indexing
slides.markdown:
Raw text isn't indexed as-is — it goes through an analysis pipeline first. **Tokenization** splits text into individual terms ("the cat sat" → `["the", "cat", "sat"]`), handling punctuation, case, and language-specific rules. **Stemming** (or lemmatization) reduces words to a common root so "running," "runs," and "ran" can all match a search for "run" — without it, a search engine treats them as unrelated terms. **Stop word removal** drops extremely common words ("the," "a," "is") that appear in nearly every document and add storage cost without adding search value.

This pipeline runs on both documents at index time and on the query at search time — using different analyzers on the two sides is a common bug (covered as a pitfall next).

slides.sectionTitle: Posting lists and how a query intersects them
slides.markdown:
Each term's list of matching documents is called a **posting list** (often storing document IDs plus extra data like term frequency or position). A multi-word query like "cat ran" fetches the posting list for "cat" and the posting list for "ran," then **intersects** them — keeping only document IDs present in both — to find documents containing both terms.

Posting lists are usually stored sorted by document ID specifically so this intersection can run efficiently (a merge-like walk over two sorted lists) instead of a nested loop. For an `OR` query, the engine unions the lists instead of intersecting them.

This is why the inverted index scales: a query touches only the posting lists for its own terms, never the full document collection.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: building a tiny inverted index
Compare: inverted index vs a B-tree index for text search
slides.markdown:
Both are indexes, but they're built for different query shapes.

| | B-tree index | Inverted index |
|---|---|---|
| Optimized for | Exact match, range, sort order | "Contains this term," ranked relevance |
| Key | A column value (e.g. `user_id`) | A tokenized term |
| Multi-term queries | Not applicable | Intersect/union posting lists |
| Typical store | Relational database | Search engine (Lucene, Elasticsearch) |
| Weak spot | Can't search inside free text | Overkill for exact-value lookups |

**How to decide:** if you're filtering or sorting on a whole column value, use a B-tree. If you're matching on words *inside* a text field, ranked by relevance, that's exactly what an inverted index is for — the two aren't competitors, most systems use both for different fields.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: indexing without normalization, so "Run" and "running" never match
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I built an inverted index, so search should just work now."

**Why it's wrong:** an inverted index built from raw, unprocessed tokens indexes "Run," "run," and "running" as three completely unrelated terms — different case, different word form. A user searching "run" gets zero results for a document that only contains "Running," even though a human would call that an obvious match.

**Correct model:** normalization (lowercasing, stemming/lemmatization) has to run at both index time and query time, using the *same* analyzer on both sides. Skipping normalization doesn't just miss edge cases — it silently breaks the common case of matching different grammatical forms of the same word.
